subject: biology
title: Temperature Regulation
summary: Temperature regulation is the body's ongoing balancing act to hold core temperature near 37°C (98.6°F) no matter what's happening outside. Explore how the hypothalamus senses temperature like a thermostat, then triggers sweating and vasodilation to cool down or shivering and vasoconstriction to warm up — a negative feedback loop that keeps the body in balance.

compareCandidate.label: Endotherms vs. ectotherms
compareCandidate.description: Humans are endotherms ("warm-blooded") — we generate our own internal heat through metabolism and actively regulate it with responses like sweating and shivering. Ectotherms ("cold-blooded") animals like reptiles instead rely on external heat sources and behaviors, such as basking in the sun or seeking shade, to control body temperature.

plainLanguageExplanation: Your body is like a house with a smart thermostat. No matter if it's freezing outside or blazing hot, a house with a good thermostat keeps its inside temperature steady. Your body does the same thing — it works hard to keep your core temperature close to 37°C (98.6°F), even when the world around you changes a lot. The "thermostat" in your body is a small structure deep in your brain called the hypothalamus. It constantly checks your blood temperature and compares it to the ideal setting. If you get too hot — from running around, exercise, or a hot day — your hypothalamus tells your sweat glands to release sweat (which cools you as it evaporates) and tells the blood vessels near your skin to widen (vasodilation), so heat can escape faster, which is why your face looks flushed when you're hot. If you get too cold, your hypothalamus does the opposite: it triggers shivering (fast muscle twitching that generates heat as a byproduct) and narrows the blood vessels near your skin (vasoconstriction) to keep warm blood deeper inside your body, away from the cold surface. This constant balancing act — sensing, adjusting, and staying steady — is called homeostasis, and temperature regulation is one of the clearest everyday examples of it in action. Interestingly, a fever works by turning this same thermostat up on purpose: the hypothalamus's set point rises above 37°C, so even though your actual temperature hasn't dropped, your body now reads itself as "too cold" compared to the new setting — which is why you can feel chilly and shiver during a fever even while your temperature is above normal.

keyFacts.label: Normal core body temperature
keyFacts.value: About 37°C (98.6°F), though it naturally varies slightly through the day and between people

keyFacts.label: Master control center
keyFacts.value: The hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain, acts as the body's thermostat

keyFacts.label: Cooling response
keyFacts.value: Sweating (evaporative cooling) plus vasodilation (blood vessels near the skin widen to release heat)

keyFacts.label: Warming response
keyFacts.value: Shivering (rapid muscle contractions produce heat) plus vasoconstriction (blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat)

keyFacts.label: Feedback type
keyFacts.value: Negative feedback loop — the response works to cancel out the original change, pulling temperature back toward the set point

keyFacts.label: Danger zones
keyFacts.value: Body temperature that strays too far from normal for too long (heatstroke when too hot, hypothermia when too cold) can be life-threatening, which is why this system matters so much

whyItMatters: Temperature regulation isn't just a background body process — it's what lets you run around on a hot summer day, walk to school in freezing winter air, or fight off an illness with a fever, all without your organs shutting down. Enzymes and cells inside your body only work properly within a narrow temperature range, so even a few degrees of drift in the wrong direction can make you feel sick, and a large drift can be dangerous. Understanding thermoregulation also explains everyday experiences: why you shiver and your lips look pale when you're freezing, why your face gets red and sweaty after exercise, and why doctors take your temperature when you're sick. It's also the foundation for understanding fevers, heatstroke, hypothermia, and how different animals (like reptiles versus mammals) survive in very different climates.
